components.note: 非 (two things back-to-back) — 靠 relates to leaning against or relying on something
告 (gào) gives a sound distantly related to 靠's reading kào, having drifted apart over time
辶 (walking/movement) — relates to 近's meaning 'near, close,' a short distance to walk.
斤 (jīn) gives a sound hint — 近 is pronounced jìn, sharing the same base sound with a different tone.

example.hanzi: 别靠近那条狗,它可能会咬人。
example.pinyin: Bié kàojìn nà tiáo gǒu, tā kěnéng huì yǎo rén.
example.english: Don't get close to that dog, it might bite.
example.fact: 靠 alone means "to lean against, to rely on" (as in 靠墙, "leaning against the wall") — combined with 近 ("near"), 靠近 literally means "to lean in near," a physical sense of approaching that also underlies the more abstract 靠得住 ("reliable," literally "able to be leaned on").

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
刂 (a knife) — 刻 relates to carving with a blade
亥 (hài) is the historical phonetic element; it no longer closely matches 刻's modern reading kè

example.hanzi: 现在是三点一刻。
example.pinyin: Xiànzài shì sān diǎn yí kè.
example.english: It's a quarter past three now.
example.fact: 刻 as a unit of time literally means "to carve, to engrave" — a name traditionally traced back to the graduated marks carved onto ancient water clocks (刻漏) used to track the passing of quarter-hours, the same character root behind 时刻 ("moment") and 深刻 ("profound," literally "deeply carved").

components.note: 见 (to see) — 规 originally named a craftsman's compass, a tool used to observe and measure circles, extended to 'rule, regulation.'
夫 (fū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from guī.
贝 (a shell, an ancient form of currency/valuables) — represents the property or standards that rules protect.
刂 (a knife) — depicts laws being carved or inscribed onto a slate, the source of 则's meaning 'rule, standard.'

example.hanzi: 请大家遵守比赛规则。
example.pinyin: Qǐng dàjiā zūnshǒu bǐsài guīzé.
example.english: Everyone please follow the rules of the competition.
example.fact: 规 originally named a craftsman's compass — a tool for drawing perfect circles — while 则 (built from 贝, a shell once used as currency, plus a knife 刂ancient laws being inscribed) named an inscribed standard; 规则 pairs "measuring tool" with "inscribed standard" into today's word for "rule."

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我昨天接到了一个奇怪的电话。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zuótiān jiēdào le yí gè qíguài de diànhuà.
example.english: I received a strange phone call yesterday.
example.fact: 接到 pairs the verb 接 ("to receive, to catch") with the result complement 到 ("to arrive, to reach") — a common Mandarin pattern where a directional or result verb tacked onto a main verb confirms the action actually succeeded, the same construction behind 看到 ("to catch sight of") and 听到 ("to hear").

components.note: 亻 (a person) — someone receiving something
寸 (a hand) — a hand handing something over
屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'

example.hanzi: 为了通过考试,他付出了很多努力。
example.pinyin: Wèile tōngguò kǎoshì, tā fùchū le hěn duō nǔlì.
example.english: To pass the exam, he put in a lot of effort.
example.fact: Unlike plain 付 or 花钱 ("to spend money"), 付出 is reserved for paying out something abstract — effort, time, a price, a sacrifice — almost never actual cash; for handing over money in a transaction, Chinese instead uses 付 or 支付.

components.note: 阝 (a mound or place) — 队 pictures people gathering together.
人 (person) — people gathering in one place gave 队 its meaning 'a team' or 'a line/queue.'
贝 (shell/money — cowrie shells were historically used as currency) — 员 originally related to counting or officials responsible for accounts, later broadening to mean 'member' or 'personnel.'

example.hanzi: 每个队员都要参加训练。
example.pinyin: Měi gè duìyuán dōu yào cānjiā xùnliàn.
example.english: Every team member has to attend training.
example.fact: 员 is one of Mandarin's most productive occupational suffixes — attach it to almost any group or role and it names a member of it (队员 "team member", 学员 "trainee", 演员 "actor", 售货员 "salesperson") — a pattern that traces back to 员's old sense of a counted, registered official.

components.note: Cloth/towel — hats are made of cloth.
Gives the sound mào, matching the character's reading.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 外面很冷,记得戴帽子。
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn hěn lěng, jìde dài màozi.
example.english: It's cold outside, remember to wear a hat.
example.fact: Beyond the literal hat, 帽子 shows up figuratively as an unwanted label pinned on someone — 扣帽子 ("to slap a hat on someone") describes unfairly branding a person with a damning accusation, an idiom especially associated with the political campaigns of Cultural-Revolution-era China.

components.note: 办 (to manage/handle) — 协 relates to people working together to manage something
十 (shí) gives a sound distantly related to 协's reading xié, having drifted apart over time
讠 (speech) — relates to 议's meaning 'to discuss, deliberate; opinion.'
义 (yì) gives the sound — 议 is also pronounced yì, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 两家公司签了一份协议。
example.pinyin: Liǎng jiā gōngsī qiān le yí fèn xiéyì.
example.english: The two companies signed an agreement.
example.fact: 协议 also does technical duty in computing as "protocol" (网络协议, "network protocol") — the same word covers a diplomatic pact and a data-transfer standard, since both describe two parties agreeing in advance on a shared set of rules.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
卩 (a person) — the one being dressed.
月 (a garment shape) — a hand 又 placing a coat on the person, giving 服 its meaning 'clothes; to obey, submit.'

example.hanzi: 我花了很长时间才说服他改变主意。
example.pinyin: Wǒ huā le hěn cháng shíjiān cái shuōfú tā gǎibiàn zhǔyi.
example.english: It took me a long time to persuade him to change his mind.
example.fact: 服 by itself already means "to submit, to yield" (as in 服从, "to obey"), so 说服 is literally "to talk someone into submission" — fitting for a character whose own picture shows a hand fitting a garment onto a person, an image of being outfitted into compliance.

components.note: A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.
冂 depicts a boundary or border enclosing an area.
土 (earth/land) — the land enclosed within the border.
口 here depicts a well within that land — together giving 周 its early meaning of a bounded territory, and later 'circumference, week, the Zhou dynasty.'

example.hanzi: 上周我们去爬山了。
example.pinyin: Shàngzhōu wǒmen qù páshān le.
example.english: Last week we went hiking.
example.fact: 上 here isn't "above" but "previous" in a time sequence — the same 上 shows up in 上个月 ("last month") and 上次 ("last time") — while its mirror 下 marks "next" (下周, 下个月), a spatial up/down pair repurposed as Mandarin's default before/after marker for time.

components.note: 司 depicts a person with a raised arm giving orders — an official directing others, giving rise to the meaning 'to manage' or 'to take charge of.'
木 (wood) — 机 originally referred to a wooden device or machine, such as a loom.
几 depicts a small table or stool — combined with 木 (wood), the character pictured a wooden machine or mechanism.

example.hanzi: 出租车司机很热情地跟我聊天。
example.pinyin: Chūzūchē sījī hěn rèqíng de gēn wǒ liáotiān.
example.english: The taxi driver chatted with me warmly.
example.fact: 司 alone is a very old word meaning "to take charge of, to manage" (as in 司令, "commander"), so 司机 literally means "the one in charge of the machine" — a fitting compositional image once cars, trains, and other engines started being called 机.

components.note: 扌 (hand) shows 搜 relates to physically searching for something.
叟 (sǒu) gives a sound close to sōu, differing mainly in tone.

example.hanzi: 警察搜查了整栋大楼。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá sōuchá le zhěng dòng dàlóu.
example.english: The police searched the entire building.
example.fact: 搜查 carries a formal, official register — used for police or authorities conducting a thorough, sanctioned search, often requiring a warrant (搜查令) — while the everyday, neutral verb 找 is simply "to look for" something you've misplaced.

components.note: 厂 (chǎng) gives a hint of the sound — 产 is pronounced chǎn, nearly identical apart from the final consonant.
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 这个决定可能会产生严重的后果。
example.pinyin: Zhège juédìng kěnéng huì chǎnshēng yánzhòng de hòuguǒ.
example.english: This decision could give rise to serious consequences.
example.fact: 产生 fuses "to produce" (产) with "to be born, to grow" (生) into a verb reserved for abstract outcomes — feelings, effects, problems — while 生产, the same two characters in reverse order, names the concrete industrial sense "to manufacture," a tidy example of character order alone splitting a pair into two different words.

components.note: 日 (sun/day) — relates to 时's meaning of 'time, season'; the phonetic part of the character was later replaced by 寸 in the simplified form
亻 (person) — 代 relates to a person's place in time.
弋 (a stake used to mark or catch something) — combined with 亻 (person), 代 came to mean a 'generation' or 'era,' and 'to take the place of' someone.

example.hanzi: 我们生活在一个信息爆炸的时代。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen shēnghuó zài yí gè xìnxī bàozhà de shídài.
example.english: We live in an era of information explosion.
example.fact: 代 alone already means "a generation" (一代, "one generation") or "to take the place of" (代替) — 时代 extends that generational sense onto a whole historical span, so a 时代 is literally the length of time one "generation" or "era" occupies.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 接 relates to receiving or connecting something by hand.
妾 (qiè) gives a hint of the sound — 接 is pronounced jiē, a connection that has shifted over time.
角 (horn) — 触 originally described an animal butting or goring with its horns, extended to any physical contact.
虫 (chóng) gives a sound distantly related to chù, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 医生提醒我们尽量少接触病人。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng tíxǐng wǒmen jǐnliàng shǎo jiēchù bìngrén.
example.english: The doctor reminded us to have as little contact with the patient as possible.
example.fact: 触 by itself already means "to touch, to bump into" — its component 角 (horn) reflects an original image of an animal butting with its horns — so 接触 layers 接 ("to receive, to connect") on top to generalize that physical contact into today's broader sense of being "in touch with" people, ideas, or information.

components.note: 上 (top) — the upper edge pressing down
卜 — the lower edge, with a card squeezed between the two
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 一辆卡车堵住了整条路。
example.pinyin: Yí liàng kǎchē dǔzhù le zhěng tiáo lù.
example.english: A truck blocked the entire road.
example.fact: 卡 in 卡车 is widely believed to be a phonetic loan from English "car" — borrowed purely for its sound (kǎ) rather than any native meaning ("to jam, to block," as in 卡住) — joining other early 20th-century sound-based loanwords like 卡片 ("card") and 巴士 (bāshì, "bus").

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 抢 describes seizing or grabbing something forcefully.
仓 (cāng) is only distantly related in sound to qiǎng — both end in the -ang family, but the initial and tone have drifted apart.
Strength — force is used to take something.
Gives the sound qù, related to jié but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 那家银行昨晚被抢劫了。
example.pinyin: Nà jiā yínháng zuówǎn bèi qiǎngjié le.
example.english: That bank was robbed last night.
example.fact: Both halves of 抢劫 independently mean "to seize by force" — 抢 ("to grab, to snatch") and 劫 ("to plunder," as in 打劫, "to hold up, to rob") — stacking two near-synonymous verbs of violent taking into one word, the same reinforcing pattern seen in words like 喜欢 ("to like," from 喜 + 欢).

components.note: 石 (rock) — 碰 originally described one hard object, like a stone, striking another, giving 'to bump, to collide.'
並 (bìng) is only distantly related in sound to pèng — both use a bilabial initial (b/p), but the rhyme and tone have drifted apart.
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 我在超市碰到了我的老同学。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài chāoshì pèngdào le wǒ de lǎo tóngxué.
example.english: I ran into my old classmate at the supermarket.
example.fact: 碰到 leans toward an unplanned, chance encounter — bumping into a person or a problem by accident — while its near-synonym 遇到 stays neutral about whether the meeting was expected, and 见到 usually implies a planned visit; the core verb 碰 literally means "to bump, to collide," so a faint sense of accidental impact lingers in the word.

components.note: 礻 (an altar, related to ritual/spirits) — 神 relates to gods and spirits.
申 (shēn) gives a hint of the sound — 神 is pronounced shén, a connection that has shifted over time.
乂 depicts a hand gripping a tool.
八 here depicts a hand-axe — a father shown wielding a tool to provide for and protect the family gave 父 its meaning 'father.'

example.hanzi: 他每个星期天都去教堂见神父。
example.pinyin: Tā měi gè xīngqītiān dōu qù jiàotáng jiàn shénfu.
example.english: He goes to church to see the priest every Sunday.
example.fact: 神父 likely began as a loan-translation of the Catholic title "Father" introduced by European missionaries — 神 ("god, divine") plus 父 ("father") mirrors the address term almost word for word — distinct from 牧师, the separate word reserved for a Protestant pastor.

components.note: 见 (to see) — 规 originally named a craftsman's compass, a tool used to observe and measure circles, extended to 'rule, regulation.'
夫 (fū) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from guī.
矢 (arrow) — arrows were historically used as a measuring standard, tied to 矩's meaning 'a carpenter's square, a rule.'
巨 (jù) gives the sound — an exact match with 矩, differing only in tone.

example.hanzi: 在这个家里,吃饭前洗手是规矩。
example.pinyin: Zài zhège jiā lǐ, chīfàn qián xǐshǒu shì guīju.
example.english: In this house, washing your hands before eating is the rule.
example.fact: 规矩 literally names two carpenter's tools — 规 the compass for drawing circles, 矩 the square for drawing right angles — the same pair found in the Mencius line 不以规矩,不能成方圆 ("without compass and square, one cannot form circles and squares"), the likely classical source of 规矩's modern sense "rule, standard."

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.
A vertical line 丨 running through the middle of a box or flag 口 — a simple image for the idea of 'center, middle.'

example.hanzi: 在众多申请者之中,只有三个人被选中。
example.pinyin: Zài zhòngduō shēnqǐngzhě zhīzhōng, zhǐyǒu sān gè rén bèi xuǎnzhòng.
example.english: Among all the applicants, only three people were selected.
example.fact: 之 is a fossil of Classical Chinese still alive today as a formal linking particle — functioning much like 的 does in everyday speech — so 之中 ("...'s midst") reads as the literary-register counterpart to the plainer, more colloquial 里面 or 当中.

components.note: A pictograph of rising flames — the source of 火's meaning 'fire.'
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 我们坐火车去北京。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen zuò huǒchē qù Běijīng.
example.english: We're taking the train to Beijing.
example.fact: 火车 literally means "fire cart" — a name fixed in place by the earliest fire-driven steam locomotives, long before diesel and electric trains made the "fire" part literally inaccurate — the same naming logic behind 火柴 ("matches," literally "fire sticks").

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
讠 (speech) — 话 relates to speaking and words.
舌 (tongue) — the organ used for speaking, reinforcing 话's meaning of 'speech' or 'words.'

example.hanzi: 说实话,我不太喜欢这个计划。
example.pinyin: Shuōshíhuà, wǒ bú tài xǐhuan zhège jìhuà.
example.english: To be honest, I don't really like this plan.
example.fact: 说实话 almost always opens a sentence as a stand-alone discourse marker — much like English "honestly" or "to be frank" — signaling that a possibly blunt or unwelcome opinion is coming next, rather than literally commanding someone to "speak the truth."

components.note: 辶 (to walk) — 逃 means to escape or flee, involving movement.
兆 (zhào) gives a rhyme close to táo, with the initial shifted.
足 (foot) — 跑 describes an action done with the feet, running.
包 (bāo) gives a sound close to pǎo, sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 那只猫看到狗就赶紧逃跑了。
example.pinyin: Nà zhī māo kàndào gǒu jiù gǎnjǐn táopǎo le.
example.english: The cat ran away as soon as it saw the dog.
example.fact: 逃跑 combines two verbs of escape that emphasize different things — 逃 ("to flee, to evade," as in 逃避, "to avoid") stresses getting away from danger, while 跑 ("to run") stresses the physical act of running — so the compound reads almost like "to flee by running," reinforcing both the motive and the method.

components.note: 阝 (a variant of 邑, meaning place/settlement) — 部 relates to a division, section, or department.
咅 supplies the sound for 部 (bù); it belongs to the same phonetic family as related characters like 倍 (bèi) and 培 (péi).
门 is a picture of a double-leafed door or gate, drawn symmetrically to show two swinging panels.

example.hanzi: 这个问题不属于我们部门负责。
example.pinyin: Zhège wèntí bù shǔyú wǒmen bùmén fùzé.
example.english: This issue isn't our department's responsibility.
example.fact: 门 broadened from its literal sense "door, gate" into a common suffix marking a category or field (部门 "department", 专门 "specialized", 门类 "category") — the underlying image treats each division of an organization as its own separate "doorway" into it.

components.note: 土 (earth) — 基 relates to the ground or foundation something is built on.
其 (qí) gives a hint of the sound — 基 is pronounced jī, a connection that has shifted significantly over time.
木 (tree) — provides the base image of a tree.
一 (a line) marks the base of the trunk, highlighting the roots — giving 本 its meaning 'root, origin, source.'

example.hanzi: 这是每个员工都应该知道的基本规则。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì měi gè yuángōng dōu yīnggāi zhīdào de jīběn guīzé.
example.english: These are basic rules every employee should know.
example.fact: 基本 stacks two near-synonymous "foundation" images — 基 (a base one builds on, as in 基础) and 本 (a tree's root, as in 根本) — into one word, and it does double duty as both an adjective ("basic") and an adverb meaning "basically" (基本上 makes this adverbial sense explicit).

components.note: 屮 (a young sprout) growing up and out of 凵 (a container or pit) — a picture of something emerging, hence 'going out.'
禾 (grain) — 租 originally described tribute paid in grain.
且 here marks the payment as regular and ongoing — combined with the grain 禾, it gave 租 its meaning 'rent, tax.'
A simplified form of 車, a pictograph of a two-wheeled cart seen from above — the wheels, axle, and frame are visible in the original shape — the source of 车's meaning 'cart, vehicle.'

example.hanzi: 我们打了一辆出租车去机场。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen dǎ le yí liàng chūzūchē qù jīchǎng.
example.english: We took a taxi to the airport.
example.fact: 出租车 literally means "a vehicle rented out" (出租, "to rent out" + 车, "vehicle"), but the far more common way to talk about actually catching one in casual Mainland speech is the verb 打车 ("to hail a taxi," literally "to hit a car"); 的士, a phonetic loan from English "taxi", is the everyday term instead in Cantonese-speaking regions like Guangzhou and Hong Kong.

components.note: 八 (to divide/split apart) — represents something already split into parts.
刀 (knife) — a knife cutting already-divided pieces further, giving 分 its meaning 'to divide, to separate.'
木 (wood) — the thing being split apart.
斤 pictures an axe, the tool used to chop the wood, giving 析 its meaning 'to split, to analyze.'

example.hanzi: 请分析一下这个问题的原因。
example.pinyin: Qǐng fēnxī yíxià zhège wèntí de yuányīn.
example.english: Please analyze the reasons behind this problem.
example.fact: 析 alone already means "to split apart" — its component 斤 pictures an axe splitting the wood 木 beside it — so 分析 ("to divide" + "to split") builds the abstract idea of "analysis" out of two very concrete images of physically breaking something into pieces.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 代 relates to a person's place in time.
弋 (a stake used to mark or catch something) — combined with 亻 (person), 代 came to mean a 'generation' or 'era,' and 'to take the place of' someone.
介 (jiè) gives a sound hint — 价 is pronounced jià, sharing the same initial consonant though the vowel has shifted.

example.hanzi: 他为这次成功付出了很大的代价。
example.pinyin: Tā wèi zhè cì chénggōng fùchū le hěn dà de dàijià.
example.english: He paid a great price for this success.
example.fact: 代价 almost always names a figurative cost — sacrifice, consequence, effort — rather than a literal shop price, which is why it pairs naturally with 付出 (also in this batch) in the fixed phrase 付出代价 ("to pay a price"); for an actual price tag, Chinese uses 价格 instead.

components.note: 土 (earth/soil) — 地's original meaning is 'earth, ground'
也 (yě) gives a partial sound match for 地's other reading dì; in this grammatical-particle usage the character is instead pronounced 'de'
匸 (an enclosure or boundary) — 区 pictures a defined territory.
乂 (a mark, here representing control or division) — dividing land into bounded territories gave 区 its meaning 'district' or 'area.'

example.hanzi: 这个地区经常下雪。
example.pinyin: Zhège dìqū jīngcháng xià xuě.
example.english: This region often gets snow.
example.fact: 区 is also a standard tier of Chinese urban administration — in a city like Beijing or Shanghai, a 区 ("district") sits directly below the municipal 市 — so 地区, literally "earth" plus "district," can mean either a loose geographic area or, more formally, a specific administrative unit.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 背 refers to the back, a part of the body
北 (běi) gives a sound close to 背's reading bèi, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
Opposite/contrary — rebellion means going against something.
Gives the sound bàn, related to pàn but drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 他背叛了自己最好的朋友。
example.pinyin: Tā bèipàn le zìjǐ zuì hǎo de péngyou.
example.english: He betrayed his own best friend.
example.fact: 叛 alone already means "to rebel, to revolt" (as in 叛乱, "rebellion"), built from 反 ("opposite, contrary") plus a phonetic element — 背叛 adds 背 ("the back," extended to "to turn one's back on") to sharpen that rebellion into the specific, personal sense of betraying someone who trusted you.

components.note: 大 (a person, arms outstretched) — represents a human being.
一 (a line, here representing the sky) — drawn above a person, showing what is above them: the heavens, hence 'sky, day.'
土 (earth) — 堂 names a hall, a large room built on the ground.
尚 (shàng) gives a rhyme close to táng, with the initial shifted.

example.hanzi: 她说这个海边小镇就像天堂一样。
example.pinyin: Tā shuō zhège hǎibiān xiǎozhèn jiù xiàng tiāntáng yíyàng.
example.english: She said this seaside town is just like paradise.
example.fact: 天堂 (literally "sky hall") entered Chinese through Buddhist and later Christian loan-translation for the idea of a heavenly afterlife, and it's paired in everyday speech with its opposite 地狱 ("hell," literally "earth prison") — a sky-versus-earth contrast that echoes the up/down cosmology found across many world religions.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 拍 describes striking something lightly with the hand.
白 (bái) gives a sound distantly related to pāi, having drifted apart over time.
扌 (hand) — 摄 describes taking hold of or capturing something, as in taking a photograph.
聂 (niè) gives a sound distantly related to shè's reading, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 这部电影是在云南拍摄的。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng shì zài Yúnnán pāishè de.
example.english: This movie was filmed in Yunnan.
example.fact: 拍摄 is the formal, professional register for filming or photography — used for movies, documentaries, or news coverage — while 拍 alone is the everyday, casual verb (拍照片, "to take a photo") that any tourist with a phone would use for a quick snapshot.

components.note: 干 (originally a person) shown carrying a heavy load of grain on their back — since harvests came once a year, the character came to mean 'year.'
车 (cart) — 轻 originally described a light, nimble cart, extended to 'light (weight), gentle.'
工 (gōng) served as the phonetic base; its pronunciation has since drifted well away from qīng.
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 现在很多年轻人喜欢在网上购物。
example.pinyin: Xiànzài hěn duō niánqīngrén xǐhuan zài wǎngshàng gòuwù.
example.english: Nowadays many young people like shopping online.
example.fact: 轻 in 年轻 literally means "light (in weight)" — its component 车 preserves an old image of a light, nimble cart — so "young" in Mandarin is built on a metaphor of youth as an unburdened, light stage of life, set against its opposite 年老 ("old," carrying a sense of being weathered and worn).

components.note: 寸 (a hand) — guiding the way.
巳 (a place) — the destination being pointed toward, giving 导 its meaning 'to lead, guide, direct.'
攵 (an action/to strike) — ties to 致's sense of bringing about or causing an effect
至 (zhì) gives the sound — 致 is also pronounced zhì, an exact match

example.hanzi: 长期缺乏运动可能导致健康问题。
example.pinyin: Chángqī quēfá yùndòng kěnéng dǎozhì jiànkāng wèntí.
example.english: A long-term lack of exercise can lead to health problems.
example.fact: 导致 leans heavily toward negative or undesirable outcomes — illness, accidents, failure — while a neutral or positive causal chain more naturally takes 使 or 让 instead, which is why native speakers notice something slightly off in a sentence like 努力导致成功 ("hard work led to success") even though it's grammatically fine.

components.note: ⺼ (flesh/body) — 脸 relates to the face, a part of the body
佥 (qiān) gives a loose sound connection to 脸's reading liǎn
A short stroke placed above a longer one — a simple graphic way to show 'up' or 'above,' contrasted with 下 (down), which flips the strokes.

example.hanzi: 听到这个好消息,他脸上露出了笑容。
example.pinyin: Tīngdào zhège hǎo xiāoxi, tā liǎnshàng lùchū le xiàoróng.
example.english: Hearing the good news, a smile appeared on his face.
example.fact: 脸上 attaches the location suffix 上 ("on top of") to 脸 ("face") to name not the face itself but whatever appears on its surface — an expression, a smile, a blush — which is why Chinese almost always says a smile "appeared 脸上" rather than describing the face directly, treating expressions as things that surface on it.

components.note: 又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'
彳 (a road/step) — someone arriving on the road
寺 (a court/hall) — the destination where the visitor is welcomed

example.hanzi: 老师应该平等地对待每一个学生。
example.pinyin: Lǎoshī yīnggāi píngděng de duìdài měi yí gè xuésheng.
example.english: Teachers should treat every student equally.
example.fact: 对待 always takes a person, or something personified, as its object — how you treat a person, an issue, or an animal — and can't be used the way English "treat" sometimes is for medical care; for that sense Chinese switches entirely to 治疗.

components.note: 丶 (a dot) — represents the burning flame atop a lamp.
王 here depicts the base and stand of an oil lamp, not its usual meaning 'king' — the one who tends the flame became linked to 'master, lord, main.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 这只狗对主人非常忠诚。
example.pinyin: Zhè zhī gǒu duì zhǔrén fēicháng zhōngchéng.
example.english: This dog is extremely loyal to its owner.
example.fact: 主 by itself already carries the sense "main, principal" (主要, "main"), tracing back to a pictograph of the flame atop an oil lamp — the part everyone's eyes are drawn to — and 主人 extends that "central, principal figure" image from an object to a person: the owner, host, or master of a place.

components.note: 釆 (to distinguish/sort) — 释 relates to sorting out and clarifying, i.e. 'to explain'
睪 (yì) gives a sound distantly related to 释's reading shì, having drifted apart over time
攵 (a hand with an implement, action) — relates to 放's meaning 'to let go, release, put.'
方 (fāng) gives the sound — 放 is pronounced fàng, a close match sharing the same rhyme.

example.hanzi: 经过调查,警方释放了那名嫌疑人。
example.pinyin: Jīngguò diàochá, jǐngfāng shìfàng le nà míng xiányírén.
example.english: After the investigation, the police released the suspect.
example.fact: Beyond freeing a person, 释放 extends naturally into physics and chemistry for "to release" energy or a substance (释放能量, "to release energy") and into everyday psychology for releasing emotion (释放压力, "to relieve stress") — one verb spanning legal, scientific, and emotional registers that English usually splits across "release," "discharge," and "vent."

components.note: A drawing of a person standing with arms and legs spread wide — used to represent the idea of something being 'big' or 'great.'
行 (to go/walk) — 街 names a road where people walk and travel.
圭 (guī) gives a sound distantly related to jiē, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 周末的时候,大街上人特别多。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò de shíhou, dàjiē shàng rén tèbié duō.
example.english: On weekends, the main street is especially crowded.
example.fact: 大街 names a wide, major thoroughfare, as opposed to a narrow 小巷 or 胡同 ("alley, lane") — and the fixed phrase 大街小巷 ("big streets, small lanes") is Mandarin's idiomatic way of saying "everywhere in town," pairing the two extremes of street width to mean total coverage.

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — 箱 originally described a bamboo case or chest.
相 (xiāng) gives the sound — an exact match with 箱.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 她把所有衣服都装进了箱子里。
example.pinyin: Tā bǎ suǒyǒu yīfu dōu zhuāngjìn le xiāngzi lǐ.
example.english: She packed all her clothes into the suitcase.
example.fact: 箱's bamboo radical ⺮ reveals that the character originally named a woven bamboo chest, long before cardboard or hard-shell suitcases existed — the same radical shows up across a whole family of container words, like 篮子 ("basket"), that trace back to bamboo construction.

components.note: 耳 (ear) — the original meaning of 耶 is unrelated to its modern use, which is mainly phonetic.
阝 (a place-name element) gives a sound distantly related to yé, having drifted apart over time.
禾 (grain) — 稣 was originally tied to reviving or gathering grain.
鱼 (yú) gives a sound only distantly related to sū today, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 很多人在圣诞节庆祝耶稣的诞生。
example.pinyin: Hěn duō rén zài Shèngdànjié qìngzhù Yēsū de dànshēng.
example.english: Many people celebrate the birth of Jesus at Christmas.
example.fact: 耶稣 is a pure phonetic transliteration — 耶 and 稣 were chosen purely for their sound (yē and sū) to approximate "Jesus," with no regard for their literal meanings — the same non-meaning-based borrowing strategy used for other foreign names and loanwords like 咖啡 (kāfēi, "coffee").

components.note: 由 resembles 田 (a field) with a stem or road extending from it — pointing the way toward a source, which gave 由 its meaning of 'from' or 'cause.'

example.hanzi: 由于天气不好,比赛被取消了。
example.pinyin: Yóuyú tiānqì bù hǎo, bǐsài bèi qǔxiāo le.
example.english: Due to bad weather, the match was cancelled.
example.fact: 由于 sits at the more formal, written end of Mandarin's "because" spectrum — the kind of connector expected in a news report or official statement — while 因为 is the neutral, everyday default used just as easily in casual conversation.

components.note: 宣 depicts a grand hall (宀) with an open, radiating space inside, evoking a palace where proclamations were made.
巾 (cloth) — held in a hand, the image behind 布's meaning 'cloth' and, by extension, 'to spread out, distribute.'

example.hanzi: 校长在大会上宣布了新的规定。
example.pinyin: Xiàozhǎng zài dàhuì shàng xuānbù le xīn de guīdìng.
example.english: The principal announced the new regulations at the assembly.
example.fact: 宣 alone already carries the sense of a grand, public proclamation — its old form pictures a wide hall radiating outward, evoking a palace where royal edicts were announced — so 宣布, adding 布 ("to spread out, to distribute"), literally means "to proclaim and spread wide," fitting for announcements meant to reach a broad audience.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — a hand gripping something tightly
丸 (a pebble/pellet) — the small object held firmly in the hand
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 这个计划已经开始执行了。
example.pinyin: Zhège jìhuà yǐjīng kāishǐ zhíxíng le.
example.english: This plan has already started to be implemented.
example.fact: 执 alone means "to hold firmly, to grasp" (as in 执照, "license," literally something one holds as proof) — 执行 extends that grip onto action itself, "to hold firmly to and carry through" a plan, order, or law, distinct from 实行 which leans more toward putting a general policy into practice.

meanings: to report sth to the police

components.note: 扌 (hand) — 报 relates to taking action against someone.
卩 (a kneeling or bound person) — handling a wrongdoer and announcing the judgment gave 报 its meaning 'to report' or 'to announce.'
言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 发现有人闯入后,她立刻报警了。
example.pinyin: Fāxiàn yǒu rén chuǎngrù hòu, tā lìkè bàojǐng le.
example.english: After discovering someone had broken in, she immediately called the police.
example.fact: 警 is the root behind Mandarin's whole police/alarm vocabulary — 警察 ("police"), 警车 ("police car"), 报警 ("to report to police, to sound an alarm") — all built on a character whose phonetic component 敬 originally lent it a sense of urgent respect or caution.

components.note: The oracle-bone form has been interpreted as a bird flying up toward the sky; the meaning later shifted entirely to represent negation, 'not.'
又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 你这样算数不对,再检查一下。
example.pinyin: Nǐ zhèyàng suànshù bú duì, zài jiǎnchá yíxià.
example.english: You calculated this wrong, check it again.
example.fact: 不对 is also a common stand-alone exclamation for catching a mistake mid-sentence — much like English "wait, no" — as when a speaker corrects themselves ("不对,不对,是三点,不是两点", "No wait, it's three o'clock, not two") rather than only describing a statement as objectively false.

components.note: 宓 depicts stillness and quiet beneath a roof.
山 (mountain) — a quiet, secluded mountain gave 密 its meaning 'dense, secret, close.'
石 (stone) — 码 originally related to counting stones used for reckoning, extended to mean 'number, code.'
马 (mǎ) is an exact match for the sound of 码.

example.hanzi: 请输入你的账户密码。
example.pinyin: Qǐng shūrù nǐ de zhànghù mìmǎ.
example.english: Please enter your account password.
example.fact: 码 is Mandarin's general word for "a numerical code" — it also shows up in 号码 ("number," as in a phone number) and 条码 ("barcode") — while 密 contributes "secret, dense, close" (as in 秘密, "secret"), so 密码 literally combines "secret" with "code" into today's word for password or cipher.

components.note: 纟 (silk/thread) — 红 originally described a color of dyed silk, hence 'red'
工 (gōng) gives a loose sound connection to 红's reading hóng
⺈ (a person, bent over) — the figure whose outward expression is being depicted.
巴 — traditionally linked to desire or emotion, so together the character points to a person's expression or complexion, extended to 色's meaning 'color, appearance.'

example.hanzi: 她穿着一条红色的裙子。
example.pinyin: Tā chuānzhe yì tiáo hóngsè de qúnzi.
example.english: She's wearing a red skirt.
example.fact: Beyond the plain color, 红色 carries a heavy political charge in Mandarin — shorthand for the Chinese Communist Party and revolutionary history, as in 红色旅游 ("red tourism," visiting revolutionary historical sites) and 又红又专 ("both red and expert," a Mao-era ideal pairing political loyalty with technical skill) — a symbolic weight most color words in English don't carry.

components.note: 马 (horse) — 骗 originally described swinging up onto a horse, later extended figuratively to 'to trick, to swindle.'
扁 (biǎn) shares the rhyme -ian with piàn, and both use a bilabial initial (b/p) — only voicing and tone differ.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 那个人是个骗子,别相信他。
example.pinyin: Nàge rén shì gè piànzi, bié xiāngxìn tā.
example.english: That person is a swindler, don't believe him.
example.fact: 骗 alone means "to deceive, to swindle," and its horse radical 马 traces back to an old image of swinging up onto a horse — perhaps an unexpectedly quick trick — which later drifted into the entirely figurative sense of tricking someone out of money or trust that 骗子 carries today.
